nodes.label: Recording metadata
nodes.one_line: Describe a field recording with enough metadata — who, what, when, where, instrument, genre, rights — to be findable and usable, using a standard like Dublin Core or LCMPI MARC fields.
know_what: Dublin Core — the 15-element metadata standard (title, creator, date, coverage, format, rights…) that lets a stranger find and use a recording without asking its collector
LCMPI MARC fields — the Library of Congress Medium of Performance codes recorded in MARC catalog fields (e.g., 048) that index which instruments a recording uses, separately from genre
who/what/when/where — the core event facts: performers and roles, the piece and genre, the date, and the place, captured at recording time because they cannot be reliably reconstructed later
instrument vs genre — two distinct metadata axes (medium of performance, musical kind), each with its own vocabulary and each searchable independently
the rights statement — who owns the recording, who may hear it, and any restrictions, written into the metadata record rather than left in a separate consent file
the recording identifier — the accession-ready number (e.g., a collection prefix plus take number) that ties a file to its metadata record and its rights record
extent — the unit of description: how much material the record covers (duration, takes, participants), so the record describes one item and not a season of fieldwork
the schema mismatch — a Dublin Core record and a MARC record organize the same facts differently, so the schema is chosen to match the receiving archive, not your convenience
know_how: Record who, what, when, where, instrument, genre, and rights in the field at the moment of recording, from the slate and the conversation, not from memory after the trip
Fill a Dublin Core record for one recording — title, creator, contributor, date, coverage, description, format, identifier, rights — with each element used as the standard defines it
Assign LCMPI codes for the instruments played (MARC 048) so the item is retrievable by medium of performance in a MARC-based catalog
Write the rights status into the metadata (open, restricted, community-only, closed) matching exactly what the consultant consented to
Create one record per take or session linked to its file by identifier, so no recording exists in the archive without its description
Cross-check every metadata value against the slate and field notes; a date or name that disagrees goes back to the source before it is entered
habits: Capture metadata at recording time — slate first, record second — because 'that session' loses its dates and names within weeks
Give the place precisely (village, district, region), so future researchers can disambiguate places that share a name
When a performer is unknown, record the gap explicitly (instrument, style, region) instead of leaving a blank that reads as an oversight
Ask the consultant for the genre name in their own language, then add your analyst category as a second entry
Treat the rights field as load-bearing: an empty rights field can make a recording unusable by anyone, no matter how good the sound
nodes.checkpoint: Take one of your own field recordings and produce a Dublin Core record for it — who, what, when, where, instrument, genre, and rights each filled from the field documentation — that a cataloger can import into a standard system without asking you a single clarifying question.
nodes.common_failure: Writing metadata as an afterthought from memory weeks after the trip: the date is approximate, the performer list incomplete, and the rights field blank — so the recording is findable in name only and may be legally unusable, exactly the shelf of noise archives warn against.
sources: Library of Congress Medium of Performance Thesaurus (LCMPT) and MARC 048 field documentation
IASA TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects

nodes.label: File standards & digitization
nodes.one_line: Convert a field recording into archival file standards — WAV/BWF 96 kHz/24-bit masters, lossless or compressed access copies, checksums, named per a convention — so it survives.
know_what: WAV/BWF at 96 kHz/24-bit — the archival master format per IASA TC 04, preserving full dynamic range and headroom so every future generation copies from a complete original
BWF — Broadcast Wave Format, the WAV variant carrying a timestamp and a bext metadata chunk that lets an archive identify the file without opening it
the master/access split — one uncompressed master kept untouched plus derived access copies for listening; no one works on the master, ever
lossless vs compressed access copies — FLAC preserves every bit for working copies; MP3/AAC at 256-320 kbps serve casual listening and are never archival
the checksum — a cryptographic digest (MD5 or SHA-256) of a file used to prove a copy is bit-identical; the unit of trust in a digital archive
the naming convention — a documented pattern like collection-creator-date-take (e.g., jones_2024-06-14_t02.wav) that sorts, disambiguates, and survives transfer between systems
format obsolescence — the reason uncompressed standards win: a proprietary codec can die with its vendor, while PCM WAV decodes with no codec at all
the unprocessed master — the master is never EQ'd, noise-reduced, or normalized; processing happens only on copies, and the raw capture is preserved
know_how: Convert a field recording to BWF at 96 kHz/24-bit as the master, keeping the original capture untouched as source material if it differs in format
Derive access copies from the master — FLAC for working, MP3 at 256-320 kbps for listening — and never run processing on the master itself
Compute a checksum (MD5 or SHA-256) for every master and store the digests in a manifest file that travels with the collection
Name files per a written convention — collection, creator, date, take, extension — and record the convention in the collection documentation
Verify a transfer by recomputing checksums after copying and comparing to the manifest, instead of trusting the copy dialog or a listening test
Embed BWF metadata in the bext chunk — title, originator, date, description — so the file carries its identity even if the catalog is lost
Document the digitization chain — source, recorder, software, settings — so a future engineer can reproduce how the file was made
habits: Treat the master as a museum object: once written, it is only read, never edited
Reach for the checksum before the listening test — two files that sound identical can still differ byte for byte
Name every file as if a stranger will sort the folder without the catalog open
When a format choice is offered, pick the one with no codec dependency (PCM WAV over a proprietary codec)
Write the naming convention down before the hundredth file exists, not after
nodes.checkpoint: Take a raw field recording and produce an archival package: a BWF master at 96 kHz/24-bit with embedded metadata, FLAC and MP3 access copies derived from it, an MD5 or SHA-256 checksum manifest verified by recomputation, and every file named per your written convention.
nodes.common_failure: Doing all the work on the original: normalizing, EQing, and saving over the field capture, so the master is a processed artifact and the true recording is gone — the one irreversible mistake in the chain, because no software restores what was overwritten.
sources: IASA TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects
Library of Congress Recommended Formats Statement
PREMIS Data Dictionary for Preservation Metadata

nodes.label: Long-term preservation
nodes.one_line: Store a digital collection so it survives a decade — redundant copies, verified checksums, format migration on a schedule, no single point of failure.
know_what: redundant copies — the 3-2-1 rule: at least three copies, on two different media types, one off-site; a single drive is a bet, not a backup
verified checksums — the scheduled re-verification of stored files against the manifest, because drives decay silently and 'it was fine last year' is not a check
format migration — re-wrapping or re-encoding at-risk formats on a written schedule (every 5-10 years) so files never outlive their codec or container
no single point of failure — the design property that losing one drive, one building, or one cloud account loses nothing irreplaceable
bit rot — the physical decay of storage (magnetic, optical, flash) that corrupts copies even when nobody touches them
LTO tape — the offline archival medium with 30-year ratings that archives trust for long-term copies, versus consumer disks rated for 3-5 years
the refresh cycle — copying data onto fresh media before the old media's rated lifespan ends, on a calendar not a whim
preservation vs backup — backup guards against accidents (deleted files, ransomware); preservation guards against decay and obsolescence, a different discipline with different schedules
know_how: Set up three copies — primary working storage, a second local copy, and an off-site copy (cloud or LTO) — and document where each lives and who owns it
Run a scheduled checksum verification (quarterly or annually) comparing stored files against the manifest, and repair any mismatch from another copy
Audit the collection for at-risk formats — proprietary codecs, old containers — and migrate them on a written 5-10 year cycle, logging each migration
Keep at least one copy on media independent of the others (different technology, different vendor), so one failure mode cannot kill two copies
Write a one-page preservation plan — copies, checksum schedule, migration cycle, responsible person — and review it annually
Test restoration, not just storage: periodically read a file back from each medium and verify it, because a backup you have never restored is a rumor
Track media age and refresh before rated end-of-life — consumer disks at 3-5 years, LTO per its 30-year rating
habits: Assume every copy will fail eventually, and ask which copy you lose when it does
Put checksum verification on the calendar like a fire drill, not a good intention
When a new format appears, ask what will read it in ten years before adopting it
Treat the off-site copy as non-negotiable — a fire that takes the house takes the archive if there is only one site
Never trust a restore until you have done one; pull a random file from each copy each year and verify it
nodes.checkpoint: Write a one-page preservation plan for your collection — at least three copies on two media types with one off-site, a scheduled checksum verification cycle, and a dated format-migration schedule — then execute one full verification pass and restore a test file from the off-site copy bit-identically.
nodes.common_failure: Treating backup as preservation: one external drive (or one cloud sync) holding the only copy, never checksummed and never restored, so the first silent drive failure or deleted-folder accident destroys years of irreplaceable fieldwork with no second copy to repair from.
sources: IASA TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects
Library of Congress National Recording Preservation Plan
PREMIS Data Dictionary for Preservation Metadata

nodes.label: Collection cataloging
nodes.one_line: Catalog a small collection — accession numbers, item-level records, finding aid — so a stranger can locate a specific recording within a day.
know_what: the accession number — the unique identifier assigned when material enters a collection (e.g., AWM 2024-01), the spine that every catalog record hangs on
the accession record — the register entry logging what arrived, from whom, when, and any restrictions, the first document of ownership
the item-level record — one catalog entry per recording covering content, performers, date, place, medium, and access status, linked by accession number
the finding aid — the collection-level guide (provenance, scope, arrangement, item list) that lets a researcher navigate the collection and locate a specific recording
the archival hierarchy — fonds → series → item — the descriptive levels that tell you how much detail belongs at each layer
controlled vocabulary — the fixed terms (LCMPI for medium, a genre thesaurus, LCSH for topics) that make searching work, because free-text keywords fail at scale
the authority file — the canonical list of names (performers, ensembles, communities) with variants, so 'Nusrat' and 'Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan' resolve to one person
access restrictions in the record — the catalog marks who may use an item (open, community-only, restricted), so the catalog itself enforces consent
know_how: Assign an accession number to a new acquisition and enter it in the accession register with source, date, and restrictions, before any other cataloging
Create an item-level record per recording — content, performers, date, place, medium, duration, access status — linked to its accession number
Write a finding aid for a small collection: provenance note, scope and content summary, arrangement, and an item list a stranger can navigate
Apply controlled vocabulary (LCMPI for instruments, a genre thesaurus, LCSH for topics) instead of free-text description
Resolve performer names against an authority file, linking spelling variants to one canonical entry
Record access restrictions in each item record, so the catalog answers 'can I listen?' without opening the file
Order the collection (by date, event, or performer) before writing the finding aid, and describe that order in it
habits: Assign the accession number the day material arrives, before anything else happens to it
Catalog at the level of use: describe the item enough to find it, not so much that records take as long as the fieldwork
When two spellings of a name appear, check the authority file instead of silently creating two entries
State restrictions in every record, even when the answer is 'open' — silence reads as permission
Test the catalog with a stranger's question and fix whatever they cannot find
nodes.checkpoint: Catalog a small collection (10-20 recordings) end to end: accession numbers in a register, an item-level record per recording using controlled vocabulary, and a finding aid — then have someone who has never seen the collection locate a specific recording by performer, date, or instrument within a day using only your records.
nodes.common_failure: Cataloging for yourself instead of for a stranger: free-text notes, no accession numbers, and names spelled however the moment felt — records that let you find your own recordings but make them invisible and unsearchable to anyone else, which defeats the purpose of an archive.
sources: Society of American Archivists, Describing Archives: A Content Standard (DACS)
Library of Congress Medium of Performance Thesaurus (LCMPT)
Archive of World Music (Harvard) cataloging practice

nodes.label: Return to communities
nodes.one_line: Deliver recordings back to the source community in usable form — copies, players, community archive, screening — and hand over control of their use.
know_what: community return — delivering recordings to the source community in usable form: copies on media they can play, players if needed, screenings, and a local archive
the community copy — the physical or digital set handed over to the community without strings, distinct from the archive's preservation master
the community archive — a locally held, community-governed collection (e.g., the Ara Irititja project in central Australia), the endpoint of true return
the TK label — Local Contexts' Traditional Knowledge labels, which let communities mark how their material may be used, layered on top of legal copyright
the screening — the public playback event in the community where recordings are heard by the people who made them, often for the first time in decades
players and formats — the practical condition of return: a BWF master is not playable in a village, so the copy's format is chosen for the community's actual equipment
graduated control — the negotiated split: the community decides access for its own members, the archive holds preservation and scholarly access per agreement
the return agreement — the written document defining copies, formats, access rules, and re-return rights, signed by archive and community representatives
know_how: Prepare the community copy in a format the community's own equipment can play, and include players when the community asks for them
Organize a screening in the community — invite performers and their families, play the recordings, record reactions and corrections — as part of the return event
Negotiate the return agreement item by item: what copies go to the community, who decides access, what the archive may do with its master
Apply TK labels or a community rights statement to returned material, so community rules ride with the recordings instead of living in an inaccessible legal file
Help establish a community archive where asked — storage, cataloging help, training — rather than dropping files and leaving
Document the return itself — what was handed over, when, to whom, under what agreement — in both the archive's record and the community's own record
Hand over decision rights in the agreement: the community's permission governs access to its own recordings, including scholarly use
habits: Ask what form of return the community wants before deciding what to hand over — a screening, copies, a community archive, or all three
Test the copy on the community's player, not yours, before calling it returned
When the archive and the community disagree about a recording, resolve toward the community's decision in the agreement
Treat the screening as a research event: the reactions are evidence about the music's meaning that no other method yields
Record the return in writing and keep the agreement where both sides can find it

know_why.claim: The archive's proper end is to hand control of recordings to the source community — copies, players, and decision rights over access — because the recordings are the community's cultural property, not the collector's.
know_why.because: The recordings document music made by the community's own members, and holding them under archival authority reproduces the extractive relation fieldwork was supposed to end; a community can only use and manage what it actually controls.
know_why.disputed_by: the documentary/preservation camp — archives following IASA TC 04 and institutions like the Archive of World Music — which holds that professional custody is what keeps fragile recordings alive and accessible to scholarship, and that unconditional handover can strand material in communities without the means to preserve it; the negotiated answer is graduated control, community copies plus archive-held preservation masters.
know_why.source: Anthony Seeger, 'Ethnomusicologists, Archives, Professional Organizations, and the Shifting Ethics of Intellectual Property' (1996); Local Contexts, Traditional Knowledge (TK) Labels; Sally Treloyn & Andrea Emberly, 'Sustaining Traditions' (2014); IASA TC 04

nodes.checkpoint: Return one collection to its source community end to end: a playable copy delivered on the community's own equipment (or with players), a screening held and documented, and a signed return agreement defining access rights — with the community's permission now governing who may use the recordings.
nodes.common_failure: Delivering copies and calling it return: handing over unplayable master files, or holding a screening and walking away — no agreement, no access rights transferred, no community archive — so the community has the files but no control, and the relationship the return was meant to repair stays extractive.
sources: Local Contexts, Traditional Knowledge (TK) Labels (Jane Anderson, Kim Christen)
Anthony Seeger, 'Ethnomusicologists, Archives, Professional Organizations, and the Shifting Ethics of Intellectual Property' (1996)
Sally Treloyn & Andrea Emberly, 'Sustaining Traditions: Ethnomusicological Collections, Access and Sustainability in Australia' (2014)
IASA TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects

nodes.label: Legacy collections
nodes.one_line: Triage an undocumented legacy collection — deteriorating reels or cassettes, unknown performers — and set digitization priorities you can defend.
know_what: the legacy collection — undocumented holdings of reels, cassettes, and discs from earlier fieldwork eras (often 1950s-70s) with incomplete or lost documentation
the deterioration clock — magnetic tape's chemical and physical decay (binder hydrolysis, oxide shedding) that makes every un-digitized reel a race against time
sticky-shed syndrome — the binder breakdown on many 1970s-80s tapes that makes them shed oxide and squeal during playback; detectable on the reel, temporarily treatable
baking — the temporary fix (e.g., 50-55°C for several hours in a dehydrator) that re-bonds sticky-shed tape for a few playbacks, long enough to digitize
digitization priority — the triage ordering: at-risk media first (deteriorating, playback-obsolescent formats), then documented items, then the rest
the unknown-performer problem — reels with no labels or logs, whose identification may require consulting the community, since the music itself rarely names itself
the defensible priority — a written digitization order justified by risk, documentation value, and community interest, not by which reel is on top of the pile
IASA TC 04 risk categories — the guidelines' ranking of audio carriers by preservation urgency, the field's standard triage frame
know_how: Survey the collection first: inventory every item — format, condition, labels, any documentation — before touching a playback machine
Rank items by IASA TC 04 risk criteria — media type, physical condition, playback obsolescence — and write the digitization order with a rationale for each decision
Test a suspect reel for sticky shed (a short playback pass, listening for squeal and watching for oxide) and bake it before attempting the full transfer
Digitize at-risk items first at archival standard (BWF 96 kHz/24-bit, higher for damaged sources), documenting the playback chain for each
Pair each digitized item with whatever documentation exists, marking gaps (unknown performer, no date) explicitly rather than filling them by guess
Consult the community for identification where possible — an unknown voice may be recognized by elders, converting a gap into documentation
Keep the original medium after digitization, stored for the record, and log its condition for the next review
Maintain the digitization log — item, format, playback equipment, operator, checksum — so the collection's provenance survives the transfer
habits: Triage by risk, not by interest — the deteriorating reel beats the fascinating one, every time
When a label is missing, write 'unknown' in the record rather than inferring from the music, which corrupts the archive
Bake only when the tape shows sticky shed, and never as routine — heat is a risk that must be earned
Assume undocumented reels need community help to identify, and plan the consultation into the project
Keep the survey document current — the collection changes with every playback and every digitization
nodes.checkpoint: Triage a legacy collection of 20+ items: complete an item-by-item inventory with condition assessments, produce a written digitization priority list ranked by IASA TC 04 risk with a rationale for each decision, and digitize the top three at-risk items to BWF with checksums and a playback-chain log.
nodes.common_failure: Digitizing whatever is on top of the pile — usually the accessible, labeled items — while the deteriorating, undocumented reels decay unplayed: the collection's most at-risk material survives last, and sticky-shed tapes cross the point of no return before anyone tests them.
sources: IASA TC 04, Guidelines on the Production and Preservation of Digital Audio Objects (carrier risk assessment)
IASA TC 05, Handling and Storage of Audio and Video Carriers
Association for Recorded Sound Collections (ARSC) Guide to Audio Preservation
